Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 548 matches in 194 texts. The retained evidence covers involuntary reaction, spoken appraisal, answer to a one-word question, answer concerning an abbot's public function, and an adversarial interview. Formula searches yielded no corpus-wide verbal definition. Family revalidation against “tongue; capacity to speak” (舌頭) and the “broad, long tongue-mark” (廣長舌相) supports one action sense: reaction and deliberate answer are different deployments of the same bodily act, not different things under depth-gate item 8.

Senses.Explanation: Sticking out the tongue is a narrated bodily response of surprise, acknowledgement, or reaction within an encounter. The Chan record repeatedly makes this visible gesture part of public encounters, but does not give it one invariant emotional gloss. Huangbo involuntarily sticks out his tongue (不覺吐舌, “without realizing it, stuck out his tongue”) on hearing that Baizhang was deaf for three days after Mazu's shout. Elsewhere a visitor sticks out his tongue and says, “truly a dragon-elephant”; an unnamed monastic leaves with his tongue out after a rebuke; and a later monk says that Huangbo Xiyun's gesture shows he has been caught out. Masters also deliberately use the action as an answer: Nanyuan sticks out his tongue when asked for “one word,” and Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what his appearance as abbot is for. Thus the ordinary bodily gesture is bent into an answer or demonstrative act in the teaching hall as well as remaining a recorded reaction; the texts themselves decide its local force, and this entry does not assign one motive to every occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: The forge and bellows are the furnace apparatus that heat and work metal. Chan masters turn the workshop into the place where people are tested and transformed: dull iron crowds the forge, a questioner is challenged to stand at the furnace without avoiding its fire, and severe teachers or encounters are called an evil forge paired with hammer and tongs. The image names pressure and working heat, not a monastery's literal smithy in these cases.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “chasing the clod.” In the corpus it belongs to a recurrent animal comparison: “the lion bites the person; the hound chases the clod.” The phrase appears as an appraisal after exchanges and in admonitions such as “you must be a lion that bites the person; do not imitate the hound chasing the clod.” Related forms call people “mad dogs chasing the clod” and say “chasing the clod and tracking the scent does not yet make a good dog.” The hound and mad-dog variants share one literal image and one corpus use; they are not separate senses.
